Yes. Having lost the account once, we do not get to choose the flattering half. The attrition number stays in.

Good morning, Izabel. It is Sofia, with the numbers the writer asked for, so nothing in the case study is guesswork. Start with the pain point, because that is what the reader remembers: Meridian's warehouse could not trust a sensor that stopped reporting. We took the worst month, February, as the baseline, and we agreed on three metrics with David: uptime, defect rate and time to replacement. Here is what the numbers say. Adoption of the new dashboard climbed from thirty-one percent in January to ninety-four percent in May. Attrition, which had reached two accounts in the quarter of the failure, is now at zero. Implementation was slow on purpose; onboarding forty warehouse operators took us three weeks, and the findings show they trusted the weekly report more than the hardware. The payback period on the firmware rebuild is eleven months. Expensive, yes, but far cheaper than losing the account. Publish all of it, including the numbers that do not flatter us. That is the whole reason the study is credible.

Izabel, it is David Chen at Meridian. Your writer sent me the draft of the case study, and I have read it twice. I will approve it, and I will give you the testimonial, but I want you to know why. It is not because the recovery was fast, because it was not. It is because you published the numbers that made you look bad, right next to the ones that made you look good. The proof of concept arrived before the full shipment, exactly as you said it would. My operators were onboarded properly, not left with a manual. And when I asked for the findings, you sent me the whole file, not a summary. So here is my line, and you may quote it: they told me the date, and then they met it. Send the final version to my legal team by Friday and we will sign off on it. And Izabel, treat this file as a best practice. Do the next account the same way.
